issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Simplify lookup of parsed TypeName in metadata
comments:
I have filled this proposal based on my experience with implementing lookup of parsed TypeName in tools https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/101767.

@adamsitnik Any thoughts about this API?

ECMA-335 6th edition §II.22.14 says

> The full name of the type need not be stored directly. Instead, it can be split into two parts at any included “.” (although typically this is done at the last “.” in the full name). The part preceding the “.” is stored as the *TypeNamespace* and that following the “.” is stored as the *TypeName*. If there is no “.” in the full name, then the *TypeNamespace* shall be the index of the empty string.

The proposed GetMetadataNamespaceAndName() API looks like it could easily mislead callers into not recognizing types whose names have been split at a “.” other than the last one.

Good point. .NET Framework and .NET Core never followed this rule in practice. The full type name is expected to be split in namespace + name using [this algorithm](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ee93104aa0e7ac77ca7e4c6db9873356a9e3e622/src/coreclr/utilcode/namespaceutil.cpp#L92-L106). We may want to add a note to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/design/specs/Ecma-335-Augments.md .

>  Returns (unescaped namespace, unescaped name) tuple for simple types. 

Does it always return `Name` or `FullName`? Or does it depend on the nested vs non-nested?

> tuple

This particular library can be consumed by Full Framework apps and they often struggle to use `ValueTuple` (https://github.com/dotnet/BenchmarkDotNet/issues/895, https://github.com/dotnet/BenchmarkDotNet/issues/667)

> Throws exception otherwise.

I see why low level metadata parsers need that, but I find it too specific to particular use case.

What would we benefit from exposing such public API?

> Does it always return Name or FullName? Or does it depend on the nested vs non-nested?

For non-nested types, it returns unescaped FullName split into name and namespace.
For nested types, it returns unescaped Name (nested types do not have namespace)

> This particular library can be consumed by Full Framework apps and they often struggle to use ValueTuple

I do not mind changing this to whatever else API review prefers; or expose the static helper methods instead.

> I see why low level metadata parsers need that, but I find it too specific to particular use case.

System.Reflection.Metadata is a library for low-level metadata readers. Every tool or library that reads metadata in its entirety using this library needs this functionality. Every shipping `TypeName` use in this repo needs it so far.

Also, I was looking at converting https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/71abc26cf8f14f5d15665d7f580365ddfa296921/src/libraries/System.Reflection.MetadataLoadContext/src/System/Reflection/TypeLoading/General/Helpers.cs#L293-L330 to use TypeName. It would need to include the .cs files with the static helper methods in yet another place if I do that.
Update the proposal at the top. I think it is a better starting point for the API review discussion.
Moving to v10 since we have reached the "feature complete" milestone; this is still on the API review backlog.

thank you for adding the remarks! 👍
Done.

Is there test coverage for parsing a nested types with namespace e.g. `TypeName.Parse("a.b+c.d")`?

What is `TypeName.Parse("a.b+c.d").Namespace` going to return?

I guess it will return `a.b+c` which is obviously wrong. I didn't know this syntax is supported, TIL!

I think it should return `a`, because the reflection APIs seem to ignore the namespace in the nested type. Passing ``System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary`2+MyRandomNamespace.Enumerator`` to `Type.GetType` returns the expected result, while if I flip the namespaces it returns `null`.
Updated to return `a` in your example.

> Passing System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary`2+MyRandomNamespace.Enumerator to Type.GetType returns the expected result

.NET Framework throws exception in this case. This looks like a bug in .NET Core - regression introduced by rewrite of the type name parser in C#. I do not think that the parser should be silently dropping any significant part of the input to the floor.

> Updated to return a in your example.

I think that the behavior for my example should be:
- Namespace returns "c", Name returns "d"
or
- Namespace returns empty string, Name returns "c.d"

I think the former option (Namespace returns `c`, Name does not change) makes more sense and will update the PR.

There's also the question of what `a.b+c.d+e` will return, and I think the answer should be `c` as well.
Done.

> a.b+c.d+e will return, and I think the answer should be c as well.

If it returns `c`, how does one distinguish between `a.b+c.d+e` and `a.b+c.d+c.e`?

I have been looking at handling of namespaces of nested types throughout the system. It seems that the system as a whole assumes that the nested types do not have namespaces. Would it best to avoid all handling of namespaces for nested types and treat the nested type name as a name without namespace even when it has a dot in it?

`a.b+c.d` -> Name: "c.d", Namespace: throws InvalidOperationException
`a.b+c.d+e` -> Name: "e", Namespace: throw InvalidOperationException

Alternatively, type.Namespace can return the outer most namespace instead of throwing to match reflection. However, it seems to be a pit of failure. Namespaces for nested types do not make sense. We have opted to throw InvalidOperationException in situations like this in the Typename APIs. For example, Typename.GetElementType throws InvalidOperationException, but the matching reflection API returns null.
Updated `GetNamespace` to throw.
FWIW I am supportive of the "throw" decision for nested types. And I wish things like `a.b+c.d` were illegal ;)

Can me make the `string className, string assemblyName` constructor private, so that it is hard to call it by mistake from random places? (If it is private, it can be only called from within the TypeLoadException implementation.)
Done, and suppressed the suggestion to remove the constructor.
